The mental model: think in three layers

Before any tool, hold these three layers in your head separately. They are different problems with different solutions:

Layer 1 — Design language (the rules). Colors, type, spacing, motion curves, the "feel." Lives in one markdown file. Doesn't move, doesn't animate. Defined once, referenced forever.

Layer 2 — Static composition (the look). Where things sit on the page, sizes, hierarchy, what's grey vs chromatic. This is what Claude Design produces well. Think of it as a frozen frame.

Layer 3 — Motion & interaction (the magic). The box rotation, the funnel transition, the head parallax, the dot-grid reacting to cursor. Claude Design does not do this layer. This is Claude Code with Three.js, GSAP, and your skill files. You design the static state in Claude Design, then Claude Code brings it to life.

Mixing these layers up is the #1 reason people get frustrated with AI design tools. Keep them separate and the workflow gets simple.

Phase 0 — Asset prep and design language (one session, ~60–90 min)

This is the most important phase. Skip it and everything downstream is wobbly. Do it well and the rest is mechanical.

Step 0.1 — Generate the head's depth/alpha/roughness maps now.

Your Aesthetic_Head_Resemblance.png is the hero asset. Lando Norris's site uses 5 maps for the head: diffuse, alpha, depth, roughness, normal. You need at minimum diffuse + alpha + depth for the V1 effect (the others are polish).

Easiest path: use a free depth-estimation tool. Two options:

Depth Anything V2 (huggingface space) — drag your PNG in, download the depth map. Free, takes 10 seconds.

MiDaS via the same Hugging Face — older but reliable.

For the alpha, just open the PNG in any tool (even Preview/Photoshop/Photopea) and export a black-silhouette/white-background version. If your head already has a transparent background it's even simpler — you already have the alpha.

Save all three as: head_diffuse.webp, head_depth.webp, head_alpha.webp in an /assets/head/ folder. WebP because that's what Lando used and it's 3-5x lighter than PNG.

Step 0.2 — Pick exactly two fonts and write them down.

Your reference Image 3 is a font called Chrononodes (or in that family — geometric, technical, slightly futuristic). For the actual website, two safe free choices that capture that vibe:

Display / headlines / "JAYON K VINOD": Geist Mono or JetBrains Mono or Space Grotesk (all free on Google Fonts). Geist Mono is my pick — same family Vercel uses, very current, technical-but-readable.

Body / descriptions / commit messages: Inter or Geist (sans). Inter is the safe bet.

Don't overthink this. The exact font matters less than picking two and sticking to them everywhere.

Build it as a Three.js scene (no R3F, vanilla Three.js inside a React component is fine) using a single plane geometry with a custom shader. The shader samples the diffuse texture but offsets the UV based on the depth map and the cursor position, creating a subtle 3D parallax effect on mouse move. Use the alpha map to mask out the background.

Constraints:

Subtle effect — max 0.02 UV offset. Lando-style restraint, not exaggerated.

The head sits on the same dot-grid background as the rest of the brain page.

60fps target. Use requestAnimationFrame, don't recreate geometry per frame.

Mobile fallback: on touch devices, ignore parallax — show the static image.

Do not touch the rest of the page yet. Just the head.

Step 2.3 — Next prompt: the reactive dot-grid.

Once the head works:

Now add the reactive dot-grid background per design-system.md section 6 ("Brain page"). 24px spacing, 1.5px dots, --neutral-200 default. On cursor proximity within 100px radius, dots grow to 3px and shift to --accent-cyan with opacity 1.0. Smooth transition via lerp, not instant snap.

Use Canvas2D, not Three.js — it's lighter and the grid is 2D. Layer it BEHIND the Three.js head canvas. Mouse move drives both.

Performance: render only on requestAnimationFrame when mouse is moving + 500ms decay; otherwise the canvas is static.

Step 2.4 — Wire up hover states for the half-page split.

The brain page has an invisible vertical split down the middle. When the cursor is on the LEFT half, fade in a very subtle warm gradient (mix of --accent-magenta and --accent-orange at 0.04 opacity) on the left half. When on the RIGHT, fade in a cool gradient (--accent-cyan + --accent-blue at 0.04 opacity) on the right.

Also: tint the head's chromatic edges to lean warm/cool based on cursor side. The head shader takes a "side" uniform (-1 to 1). Use it to bias the chromatic aberration toward warm or cool.

No click handlers yet. Just hover ambience.

Alpha map — A black-and-white image that defines the silhouette. White = "show this pixel," black = "this is background, hide it." Lets us cut the head out cleanly from any background.

WebM — The video equivalent of WebP. Much smaller than MP4, plays natively in all modern browsers. We convert your cosmos GIF to webm.

woff2 — The compressed font format browsers use. When you download from Google Fonts, you get woff2 files.

Why this step

The metallic chromatic head is the visual centerpiece of your entire portfolio. If you do nothing fancy with it, it's a flat image — pretty, but static. With one extra file (a depth map), the same image gains subtle 3D depth that responds to your cursor.

This is the exact trick Lando Norris's website uses, and it's the highest reward-to-effort ratio in your whole project. One small grayscale file unlocks the whole effect.

We generate it now, in Phase 0, because:

Once it's in your /assets/head/ folder, every later phase just uses it. No going back.

It takes 5 minutes.

Concepts

What a depth map actually is, in plain English:

Imagine your head photo, but instead of color, every pixel encodes "how close is this part of the face to the camera?" The output is a grayscale image:

White pixels = closest to the camera (the tip of the nose, the front of the forehead)

Black pixels = furthest from the camera (the background, the edges of the silhouette)

Gray pixels = somewhere in between (the cheeks, the ears, the neck)

Once we have this map, a shader can read it and say "for pixels that are 'closer' (white in the depth map), shift them more when the cursor moves; for pixels that are 'further' (dark in the depth map), shift them less." The brain reads that as 3D depth even though the image is technically still flat.

Why we generate it with AI instead of by hand:

Making a depth map by hand is hours of painting in Photoshop. AI does it in 3 seconds because it's been trained on millions of photos with known depth. The model literally guesses depth from a single 2D image. For our use case the AI version is more than good enough.

The model we'll use: Depth Anything V2.

This is the current best-in-class open-source depth estimation model (released by ByteDance in 2024). It's on Hugging Face Spaces, runs for free, no account required.

Step 3 of Phase 0: The alpha mask (decide approach, then generate)

Why this step

Your head_diffuse.webp shows the head on a solid black background. When we render it in the brain page later, we want just the head visible — the black background needs to disappear so the dot-grid behind it shows through.

A shader needs to know, for every pixel: "is this head, or is this background?" That's what an alpha mask is. It's a black-and-white image where white = "show this pixel" and black = "hide this pixel as transparent."

The alpha mask itself doesn't render visually — it's a behind-the-scenes file the shader reads to know what to cut out.

Concepts

Alpha channel — Most images have 3 channels: red, green, blue. PNG and WebP support a 4th: alpha (transparency). 0 alpha = fully transparent, 255 alpha = fully opaque. We can store this either as a separate grayscale file (an "alpha map") or built into the diffuse image itself (a transparent PNG/WebP).

Two ways to do the same thing:

Approach A: Bake transparency into the diffuse image. Remove the black background directly from head_diffuse.webp, giving it a real transparent background. No separate alpha file needed. Shader uses the alpha channel of the diffuse texture.

Approach B: Separate alpha map. Keep head_diffuse.webp as-is, generate a separate black-and-white head_alpha.webp. Shader reads two textures.

Approach A is simpler in every way for our case. Fewer files to load, fewer textures for the shader to manage, one source of truth for "what is the head." The Lando Norris site uses Approach B because they're doing more complex multi-pass rendering, but for our subtle-parallax effect Approach A is cleaner. We'll go with A.

Background removal — The actual task is removing the black background and replacing it with transparency. Three ways to do this:
